AdaSplash-2: Faster Differentiable Sparse Attention

Nuno M. T. Gonçalves Affiliation: Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa Affiliation: Instituto de Telecomunicações Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Hugo Pitorro Affiliation: Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa Affiliation: Instituto de Telecomunicações    Vlad Niculae Affiliation: Language Technology Lab, University of Amsterdam    Edoardo M. Martins Affiliation: Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa Affiliation: Instituto de Telecomunicações Affiliation: TransPerfect Affiliation: ELLIS Unit Lisbon    Marcos V. Abstract

Sparse attention has been proposed as a way to alleviate the quadratic cost of transformers, a central bottleneck in long-context training. A promising line of work is α\alpha-entmax attention, a differentiable sparse alternative to softmax that enables input-dependent sparsity yet has lagged behind softmax due to the computational overhead necessary to compute the normalizer τ\tau. In this paper, we introduce AdaSplash-2, which addresses this limitation through a novel histogram-based initialization that reduces the number of iterations needed to compute τ\tau to typically 1–2. The key idea is to compute a coarse histogram of attention scores on the fly and store it in on-chip SRAM, yielding a more accurate initialization that enables fast forward and backward computation. Combined with a sparsity-aware GPU implementation that skips zero blocks with low overhead, AdaSplash-2 matches or improves per-step training time relative to FlashAttention-2 when block sparsity is moderate-to-high (e.g., >>60%), which often occurs at long-context lengths. On downstream tasks, models trained with our efficient α\alpha-entmax attention match softmax baselines at short-context lengths and achieve substantial gains in long-context settings.

1 Introduction

The self-attention mechanism in transformers constitutes a major computational bottleneck since computing and materializing the score matrix 𝑺=𝑸​𝑲⊤\bm{S}=\bm{Q}\bm{K}^{\top} incurs quadratic time and memory complexity, limiting scalability to long sequences (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Tay et al., 2022). FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2024; Shah et al., 2024) provides efficient GPU implementations that avoid this quadratic memory cost in the case of softmax attention. By making the computation IO-aware and by fusing operations over tiles that fit in on-chip fast memory, FlashAttention avoids storing intermediate scores and reduces memory complexity to linear in sequence length while achieving substantial speedups in training.

The key operation requiring efficient implementations is normalization. For a score vector 𝒔\bm{s}, softmax can be written as

softmax(𝒔)=exp(𝒔−τ𝟏),τ=log∑jexp(sj),\mathrm{softmax}(\bm{s})=\exp(\bm{s}-\tau\mathbf{1}),\quad\tau=\log\sum\nolimits_{j}\exp(s_{j}), (1)

where τ\tau is an additive log-sum-exp normalizer. This form admits stable online accumulation and makes softmax particularly amenable to single-pass, tiled GPU implementations. FlashAttention and its successors (Dao, 2024; Shah et al., 2024) exploit precisely this structure.

However, softmax attention is inherently dense as every token receives nonzero probability mass. For long inputs, this density can be undesirable—attention mass spreads over many irrelevant tokens (Veličković et al., 2025), and token representations become less distinguishable (Barbero et al., 2024)—motivating adaptive sparse alternatives. The α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } transformation (Peters et al., 2019) provides such an alternative: it is differentiable, yields exact zeros in an input-dependent way, and has been shown to improve long-context generalization relative to softmax (Vasylenko et al., 2025). Like softmax, α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } also requires computing a normalizer similar to τ\tau in (1) (to be described in §2.3); however, its evaluation is not additive and requires iterative root-finding methods. This has historically prevented α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } attention from matching optimized softmax attention kernels in end-to-end training throughput.

While AdaSplash (Gonçalves et al., 2025) has recently mitigated this problem by introducing a GPU-friendly implementation of α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } attention, the provided algorithm still requires multiple expensive passes over the attention scores to compute τ\tau. This limits efficiency, particularly in the forward pass and in moderate-sparsity regimes where sparsity is present but not extreme.

In this work, we introduce AdaSplash-2, a new and more efficient hardware-aware method for α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } attention that reduces the computational cost of normalization. As we show in Figure 1, AdaSplash-2 outperforms a highly-optimized CUDA implementation of FlashAttention-2 on moderate sparse regimes and can double the speedup at high sparsity cases. The key idea of our method is to construct a compact histogram of attention scores on the fly while streaming tiles through on-chip SRAM. This histogram yields a provable lower bound on the true normalizer τ\tau, providing a high-quality initialization that allows the subsequent root solver to converge to the exact solution in one (typically) or two iterations, without materializing dense intermediates. Our contributions include:11 1 Code available at: https://github.com/deep-spin/adasplash

  • •

    Normalization via on-chip histogram. We derive a provable lower and upper bound on the α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } normalizer τ\tau by computing a compact histogram of streamed scores entirely in on-chip SRAM, enabling fast α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } evaluation without forming dense intermediates.

  • •

    One-pass refinement with a safeguarded hybrid solver. Initialized from the histogram estimate, a single additional pass typically suffices to recover the exact normalizer τ⋆\tau^{\star} using a safeguarded hybrid solver, yielding near-single-iteration convergence in practice for α∈{1.5,2.0}\alpha\in\{1.5,2.0\}.

  • •

    Efficient exploitation of dynamic sparsity on GPU. We design an optimized attention kernel in Triton with fine-grained tiling and a lightweight bit-packed encoding of nonzero blocks, enabling input-dependent sparsity to be exploited with negligible overhead.

  • •

    Strong empirical results on synthetic and language modeling benchmarks. Our results show that AdaSplash-2 is not only faster than FlashAttention-2 on moderate sparse regimes, but also matches or outperforms standard softmax attention on short- and long-context downstream tasks.

2 Background

2.1 Hardware Performance

Modern GPUs are built for efficient parallel execution over a hierarchical memory system. High-bandwidth memory (HBM) provides large capacity but higher access latency than the smaller, faster on-chip SRAM (Jia et al., 2018). High performance therefore depends on efficient use of SRAM to reduce bottlenecks from frequent HBM traffic. GPUs run computation as kernels launched over thousands of threads grouped into thread blocks; data are staged from HBM into SRAM for computation and then written back. Kernel fusion is a core optimization that merges multiple operations into a single kernel, avoiding intermediate HBM reads/writes by directly producing final outputs. While compilers such as torch.compile can automate fusion for relatively simple operator chains (Ansel et al., 2024), attention mechanisms typically require custom strategies to reorder operations and optimize memory usage effectively.

2.2 Standard Dot-Product Attention

Given a set of matrices 𝑸,𝑲,𝑽∈ℝn×d\bm{Q},\bm{K},\bm{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} containing dd-dimensional representations for nn queries, keys and values, the dot-product self-attention at a single head is computed in the following way (Vaswani et al., 2017):

𝑺=𝑸​𝑲⊤d∈ℝn×n,𝑶=π⁡(𝑺)​𝑽∈ℝn×d.\bm{S}=\frac{\bm{Q}\bm{K}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},\quad\bm{O}=\pi\left(\bm{S}\right)\bm{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}. (2)

The π\pi transformation maps rows to normalized probability vectors, with softmax (Equation 1) being the most common choice. Crucially, the normalization τ\tau is a stable reduction along each row of 𝑺\bm{S} and can be computed online in a single pass (Milakov and Gimelshein, 2018).

FlashAttention.

To address the costs of naive attention implementations, Dao et al. (2022) introduced FlashAttention, an algorithm that avoids the materialization of intermediate quadratic attention matrices via a GPU-aware implementation of online softmax (Milakov and Gimelshein, 2018), bringing the overall memory complexity to 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}\left(n\right). The key idea of FlashAttention is to split the inputs 𝑸,𝑲,𝑽\bm{Q},\bm{K},\bm{V} into blocks, load them from slow GPU high bandwidth memory (HBM) to the fast GPU on-chip SRAM, then compute the attention output regarding those blocks and, at the end, scale the output by the right normalization factor. Later, FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2024) improved the original algorithm and effectively defined the algorithmic structure adopted by subsequent variants, such as FlashAttention-3 (Shah et al., 2024), which introduced hardware-specific optimizations for NVIDIA Hopper GPUs (e.g., TMA, WGMMA instructions, warp specialization) while preserving the same high-level algorithm.

2.3 α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } Transformation

Softmax-based attention is inherently dense, as every key receives a strictly positive weight. A principled differentiable sparse alternative is the α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } transformation (Peters et al., 2019). For α>1\alpha>1, α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } can produce sparse probability vectors, and it interpolates between softmax (α→1\alpha\to 1) and sparsemax (α=2\alpha=2, Martins and Astudillo 2016):

α​-entmax ​(𝒔)=[(α−1)​𝒔−τ​𝟏]+1α−1,\alpha\text{-entmax }(\bm{s})=[(\alpha-1)\bm{s}-\tau\bm{1}]_{+}^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}}, (3)

where [⋅]+[\cdot]_{+} is the ReLU function, and τ∈ℝ\tau\in\mathbb{R} is the (unique) normalizing constant which ensures the output is a valid probability distribution, ∑iα​-entmax ​(𝒔)i=1\sum_{i}\alpha\text{-entmax }(\bm{s})_{i}=1. This means that coordinates with (α−1)​si≤τ(\alpha-1)s_{i}\leq\tau become exactly zero. Importantly, α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } yields dynamic sparsity, where the pattern of zeros depends on the input 𝒔\bm{s}. Despite its flexibility, α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } does not have a direct closed-form solution, so computing it requires more involved methods, which we discuss next.

2.4 α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } Computation

Computing α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } is equivalent to finding the normalizing constant τ⋆\tau^{\star} satisfying f⁡(τ⋆)=0f(\tau^{\star})=0, where

f⁡(τ)≔−1+∑j=1n[(α−1)​sj−τ]+1α−1.f(\tau)\coloneqq-1+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left[(\alpha-1)s_{j}-\tau\right]_{+}^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}}. (4)

The function ff is continuous and strictly decreasing in τ\tau, hence the root τ⋆\tau^{\star} is unique (Blondel et al., 2019).

Sorting-based solvers.

For α=1.5\alpha=1.5 and α=2\alpha=2 (sparsemax), specialized solvers can be derived by sorting 𝒔\bm{s} and exploiting the fact that the support is given by the top-kk entries (Michelot, 1986; Duchi et al., 2008; Condat, 2016; Peters et al., 2019). These approaches are less attractive on GPU because sorting and support selection are expensive and hard to fuse.

Bisection (bracketing).

For general α>1\alpha>1, τ⋆\tau^{\star} can be found by a bracketing method such as bisection (Blondel et al., 2019), which only needs an interval containing the root. Let m=(α−1)​max⁡(𝒔)m=(\alpha-1)\max(\bm{s}). Following Peters et al. (2019), τ⋆\tau^{\star} satisfies

m−1≤τ⋆≤m−n1−α,m-1\,\leq\,\tau^{\star}\,\leq\,m-n^{1-\alpha}, (5)

which provides a valid initial bracket. While bisection is robust, it converges linearly and requires repeatedly evaluating ff, motivating faster refinement strategies on GPU.

AdaSplash.

Gonçalves et al. (2025) proposed a GPU-oriented implementation of α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } attention that exploits dynamic sparsity and IO-awareness. Its main contribution is a hybrid Halley-bisection solver for the normalization threshold τ⋆\tau^{\star}, combining fast local convergence with bracketing guarantees. Implemented as custom Triton (Tillet et al., 2019) kernels, AdaSplash can skip zero blocks in forward and backward passes, improving performance at very high sparsity via a naive block masking strategy. However, refining τ⋆\tau^{\star} typically requires multiple iterations, each involving additional passes over the keys. In addition, its naive block masking strategy incurs extra overhead to determine which blocks can be skipped. Our method, described next, reduces the number of iterations and introduces a lightweight scheme to skip zero blocks.

3 Our Method

We present AdaSplash-2, a hardware-aware sparse attention mechanism that achieves efficient τ\tau computation through a histogram-based approximation built entirely in on-chip SRAM. Our approach improves runtime compared to AdaSplash while maintaining the theoretical guarantees and sparsity benefits of α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax }.

3.1 Histogram Approximation

Given attention scores 𝒔∈ℝn\bm{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, our goal is to compute the threshold τ⋆\tau^{\star} such that Equation 4 satisfies f⁡(τ⋆)=0f(\tau^{\star})=0. Since α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } is invariant to adding a constant to all scores, we apply the change of variables

𝒛=(α−1)​𝒔−(m−1)​𝟏,\bm{z}=(\alpha-1)\bm{s}-(m-1)\bm{1}, (6)

obtaining max⁡(𝒛)=1\max(\bm{z})=1. We henceforth work with centered scores 𝒛\bm{z}, which restricts both the active entries and the threshold search to the unit interval (see Equation 5).

Histogram construction.

With this change of variables, we discretize the interval [0,1][0,1] into BB equal-width bins with width h=1/Bh=1/B. Formally, each score zj∈[0,1]z_{j}\in[0,1] is mapped to a bin index as follows:

b⁡(zj)=min⁡(⌊B​zj⌋,B−1).b(z_{j})=\min\!\left(\lfloor Bz_{j}\rfloor,\,B-1\right). (7)

At the same time we construct and maintain a histogram ℋ\mathcal{H} in SRAM to store bin counts,

ℋk=|{j:b(zj)=k}|,k=0,…,B−1.\mathcal{H}_{k}=\bigl|\{\,j:b(z_{j})=k\,\}\bigr|,\qquad k=0,\dots,B-1. (8)

Importantly, this representation only requires 𝒪⁡(B)\mathcal{O}(B) storage (independent of nn), and entries with zj<0z_{j}<0 are not included in the histogram since they cannot belong to the active set.

Histogram objective.

Now in objective (4), we replace each score zjz_{j} by the left endpoint of its bin. Concretely, if zjz_{j} is assigned to bin k=b⁡(zj)k=b(z_{j}), we score it by z~j≔k/B\tilde{z}_{j}\coloneqq k/B. This allows us to rewrite a discretized objective as a sum over bins:

fh​(τ)\displaystyle f_{h}(\tau) =−1+∑j=1n[z~j−τ]+1α−1\displaystyle=-1+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left[\tilde{z}_{j}-\tau\right]_{+}^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}}
=−1+∑k=0B−1∑j:b⁡(zj)=k[kB−τ]+1α−1\displaystyle=-1+\sum_{k=0}^{B-1}\sum_{j:b(z_{j})=k}\left[\frac{k}{B}-\tau\right]_{+}^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}}
=−1+∑k=0B−1ℋk⋅[kB−τ]+1α−1.\displaystyle=-1+\sum_{k=0}^{B-1}\mathcal{H}_{k}\cdot\left[\frac{k}{B}-\tau\right]_{+}^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}}. (9)

Structurally, this construction replaces the original set of scores by BB distinct values with associated counts HkH_{k}, yielding a reduced problem of size B≪nB\ll n with the same monotone structure as the exact normalization in Equation 4. In turn, this reduced problem can be solved using any algorithm developed for α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } normalization. In particular, exact solvers apply for α=1.5\alpha=1.5 and α=2\alpha=2 (see §2.4). The key difference is that, in our setting, these solvers operate on a compact histogram representation that fits entirely in SRAM, minimizing the computation overhead compared to operating on the full set of nn scores, which need to be recomputed from HBM. For completeness, we provide the corresponding solver adaptations for the histogram objective in Appendix C.3. We now formalize the approximation quality of the histogram objective and establish guarantees on the accuracy of the resulting normalization.

3.2 Theoretical Properties and Guarantees

We first show that the histogram objective yields a conservative estimate of the true normalization threshold. We then characterize how the smoothness of ff and α\alpha-entmax depends on α\alpha, motivating when safeguarded higher-order updates (e.g., Halley (Scavo and Thoo, 1995)) are appropriate.

{proposition}

[Histogram Lower Bound] Let α>1\alpha>1 and h=1/Bh=1/B be the bin width. Let ff and fhf_{h} be defined as in Equations 4 and 9. If τ⋆\tau^{\star} denotes the unique root of f⁡(τ)=0f(\tau)=0 and τh\tau_{h} the unique root of fh​(τ)=0f_{h}(\tau)=0, then:

τ⋆−h<τh≤τ⋆.\tau^{\star}-h<\tau_{h}\leq\tau^{\star}. (10)

Thus, the absolute error satisfies 0≤τ⋆−τh<h=1B0\leq\tau^{\star}-\tau_{h}<h=\frac{1}{B}.

The proof is given in Appendix B.1. This result ensures that the histogram approximation never overestimates the true threshold (τh≤τ⋆\tau_{h}\leq\tau^{\star}) and provides explicit control over the maximum approximation error through the bin width hh. In particular, the error satisfies 0≤τ⋆−τh<h0\leq\tau^{\star}-\tau_{h}<h, and the approximation converges to the true solution as B→∞B\to\infty.

Other binning approaches lead to different precision-sparsity tradeoffs. Using a right-edge strategy b⁡(zj)=⌈B⋅zj⌉/Bb(z_{j})=\lceil B\cdot z_{j}\rceil/B reverses the inequality to τh≥τ⋆\tau_{h}\geq\tau^{\star}, yielding a sparser output at the cost of potentially discarding relevant scores, while a centered approach b⁡(zj)=(⌊B⋅zj⌋+0.5)/Bb(z_{j})=(\lfloor B\cdot z_{j}\rfloor+0.5)/B may provide a more balanced approximation but does not induces any a one-sided bound guarantee. In AdaSplash-2, we adopt the left-edge binning strategy to ensure that the active support induced by τh\tau_{h} contains the true support.

Smoothness and safe higher-order refinement.

Following our histogram-based threshold initialization, we typically apply a posterior refinement step that evaluates ff and its derivatives at candidate thresholds. Because each term [zj−τ]+1/α−1[z_{j}-\tau]_{+}^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{\alpha-1}}} may be non-smooth at τ=zj\tau=z_{j}, the existence and continuity of higher-order derivatives depend on α\alpha. The next proposition makes this connection explicit, and we use it to justify when higher-order updates are well-behaved.22 2 We say f∈𝒞tf\in\mathcal{C}^{t} if ff has continuous derivatives up to t​tht\textsuperscript{th} order.

{proposition}

[Continuity of ff and α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax }.] Let f⁡(τ)f(\tau) be defined as in Equation 4 for a given α\alpha. If 1<α<t+1t1<\alpha<\frac{t+1}{t}, then f∈𝒞tf\in\mathcal{C}^{t} and, consequentially, α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } ∈𝒞t\in\mathcal{C}^{t}.

The proof is given in Appendix B.2. Proposition 3.2 clarifies which higher-order updates are numerically safe. When α∈(1,1.5]\alpha\in(1,1.5], f′′f^{\prime\prime} is bounded, so Halley updates (which use f′′f^{\prime\prime}) are numerically stable.33 3 In fact from the monotonicity of f′′f^{\prime\prime} we have |f′′​(τ)|≤n⁡(2−α)/(α−1)2|f^{\prime\prime}(\tau)|\leq n(2-\alpha)/(\alpha-1)^{2}. This is an upper bound on the Lipschitz constant of f′f^{\prime}, which by Kantorovich’s theorem controls the interval of convergence for Newton’s method (Kantorovich, 1949). When α∈(1.5,2]\alpha\in(1.5,2], f′f^{\prime} remains well-behaved but f′′f^{\prime\prime} becomes unbounded, making Newton updates more robust than Halley in practice. When α>2\alpha>2, f′f^{\prime} also becomes unbounded, and thus gradient-based methods are less stable. Based on this, we propose a new safeguarded hybrid solver: we apply Halley steps for α≤1.5\alpha\leq 1.5, Newton steps for 1.5<α≤21.5<\alpha\leq 2, and secant steps for α≥2\alpha\geq 2, always falling back to bisection whenever the proposed update falls outside the brackets. Combined with Proposition 3.2, this algorithm yields a refinement procedure that is both provably safe and fast in practice. We now outline the GPU-aware implementation of AdaSplash-2.

3.3 GPU-Aware Implementation

Our implementation orchestrates multiple coordinated passes over the key matrix, and carefully exploits memory hierarchies for data movement between HBM and SRAM. Concretely, we perform a grid loop over Tr=⌈n/Br⌉T_{r}=\lceil n/B_{r}\rceil query blocks, and for a specific iith query block 𝑸i∈ℝBr×d\bm{Q}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{B_{r}\times d} attending over key blocks {𝑲j}j=1Tc\{\bm{K}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{T_{c}} where Tc=⌈n/Bc⌉T_{c}=\lceil n/B_{c}\rceil, our method proceeds as follows.

Phase 1 (maximum).

Stream key blocks to compute the row-wise maximum mim_{i}, which is scaled by (α−1)(\alpha-1).

Phase 2 (histogram).

Using mim_{i}, we center and scale scores into [0,1][0,1] and build a BB-bin per-row histogram entirely in SRAM while streaming over key blocks. To avoid atomics, we maintain local histogram accumulators for each position (i,j)(i,j) in a query-key block and reduce them across columns after all keys are processed. Each accumulator packs BB bins (representing bin counts) into a single ww-bit integer (b=w/Bb=w/B bits per bin). A score in bin kk updates its respective local accumulator via ℋlocal←ℋlocal+2k​b\mathcal{H}^{\text{local}}\leftarrow\mathcal{H}^{\text{local}}+2^{kb}. Final bin counts are recovered using vectorized shift-and-mask operations with final reductions. Beyond fitting in SRAM, the histogram also provides an algorithmic speedup since binning implicitly orders scores by value. As a result, for α∈{1.5,2}\alpha\in\{1.5,2\}, we can apply exact solvers directly to the bin counts and recover τh\tau_{h} without an explicit sort step. The diagram in Figure 2 illustrates this process.

Phase 3 (refinement).

Starting from τh\tau_{h}, we perform a fixed number of iterations to refine τ\tau with a Hybrid solver that combines different root-finding methods (detailed in §3.2). In practice, we find that a single iteration is often sufficient for refinement due to the good accuracy of the histogram initialization. Simultaneously, we construct a binary block mask ℳ∈{0,1}Tr×Tc\mathcal{M}\in\{0,1\}^{T_{r}\times T_{c}} indicating which blocks contain non-zero attention weights. The mask is stored using bitpacking, with each group of 32 consecutive column blocks encoded in a single int32, requiring only 𝒪⁡(Tr×Tc)\mathcal{O}\left(T_{r}\times T_{c}\right) bits of memory. In contrast to AdaSplash (Gonçalves et al., 2025), this design avoids auxiliary index buffers and incurs a negligible overhead, even for long contexts.

Phase 4 (output).

Using mask ℳ\mathcal{M}, we traverse only non-zero blocks via GPU-native find-next-set (fns) instructions to compute 𝑶i=∑j:ℳi​j=1α-entmax (𝑸i𝑲j⊤,τ)𝑽j\bm{O}_{i}=\sum_{j:\mathcal{M}_{ij}=1}\alpha\text{-entmax }(\bm{Q}_{i}\bm{K}_{j}^{\top},\tau)\bm{V}_{j}, enabling 𝒪⁡(|ℳ|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{M}|) traversal complexity rather than 𝒪⁡(Tr×Tc)\mathcal{O}(T_{r}\times T_{c}).

Histogram capacity.

The bitpacking scheme naturally limits capacity since each bin can count up to 2b−12^{b}-1 items before overflow. With BcB_{c} parallel accumulators per query block, the maximum capacity is

Cmax=Bc×(2w/B−1).C_{\text{max}}=B_{c}\times(2^{w/B}-1). (11)

For our default configuration (w=64w=64, B=8B=8, Bc=64B_{c}=64), this yields Cmax=16,320C_{\text{max}}=16{,}320 keys per query block, sufficient for sequences up to 16K tokens. When sequences exceed this capacity, we employ a periodic flushing of bin counts to a Bc×BB_{c}\times B accumulator sitting in SRAM to avoid overflow. We provide more information on this in Appendix C.5.

Backward pass.

Crucially, gradients are nonzero only on the α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } support (Peters et al., 2019), we therefore reuse the block mask obtained in the forward pass to efficiently iterate only over nonzero blocks when computing the gradients with respect to queries, keys, and values. For this, we make use of native GPU instructions like fns and popc (population count) for efficient traversal. Further implementation details are presented in §C and §F, including the complete forward and backward algorithms.

4 Experiments

Our goals are to (i) verify that our histogram-based initialization for τ\tau reduces convergence steps; (ii) quantify the training-time speedups of AdaSplash-2 relative to softmax-based baselines; and (iii) study model accuracy and long-context capabilities of LLMs trained with AdaSplash-2.

4.1 Normalization Solver Analysis

Before end-to-end GPU benchmarks, we first isolate the normalization step and study how quickly different root-finding strategies recover the entmax threshold τ⋆\tau^{\star}. Concretely, we follow Gonçalves et al. (2025) and sample a Gaussian score vector of length n=4096n=4096 and compute a high-accuracy reference threshold τ⋆\tau^{\star} using an exact method (see §2.4). We then run (i) bisection; (ii) our safeguarded hybrid solver without histogram initialization;44 4 For α=1.5\alpha=1.5, our Hybrid solver empirically matches the Halley-Bisection solver of Gonçalves et al. (2025). and (iii) the same hybrid solver initialized with the histogram estimate τh\tau_{h} using B∈{4,8,16}B\in\{4,8,16\} bins. Figure 3 reports the mean absolute error averaged over 1010 runs for α=1.5\alpha=1.5.

After the first iteration, the histogram initialization places the solver orders of magnitude closer to the true root, making subsequent refinement into a near one-pass correction. As expected, more bins lead to better initial estimates.

4.2 Efficiency Benchmark

We implement AdaSplash-2, described in Section 3.1, in Triton. We compare it with FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2024) implemented in CUDA and in Triton,55 5 https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/main/python/tutorial
s/06-fused-attention.py and AdaSplash written in Triton (Gonçalves et al., 2025). A natural question is why compare with FlashAttention-2 rather than FlashAttention-3. Our efficiency experiments target NVIDIA Ampere GPUs, for which FlashAttention-2 is the reference implementation. FlashAttention-3 (Shah et al., 2024) introduces hardware-specific optimizations for NVIDIA Hopper GPUs (e.g., TMA, WGMMA instructions, warp specialization) while preserving the same high-level algorithm. This choice allows us to isolate algorithmic effects independent of such hardware tuning. We note that the low-level optimizations in FlashAttention-3 are largely orthogonal to AdaSplash-2 and can be incorporated with additional engineering effort. All runtime benchmarks are performed in a single A6000 NVIDIA GPU.

Sparsity-speed tradeoff.

Figure 1 shows runtime as a function of block sparsity for random query, key and value tensors drawn from a zero-mean Gaussian. Following Gonçalves et al. (2025), we control the block sparsity of the attention probability matrix by changing the query variance, set head dimension to d=64d=64 and use bf16 precision. AdaSplash-2 consistently outperforms AdaSplash and, unlike FlashAttention, benefits from increased block sparsity, surpassing both Triton and CUDA implementations at moderate to high sparsity regimes. In the limit, AdaSplash-2 achieves more than a 2×2\times speedup over both variants of FlashAttention-2.

Context scaling.

In this experiment, we do not hand-tune the input sparsity. Instead, we use the block-sparsity ratios learned by a 1B-parameter transformer language model at different sequence lengths (we present the full language modeling results in the next subsection). We describe how these ratios are extracted from our models and provide block sparsity heatmaps across sequence lengths in §E. Figure 4 reports the average per-step training runtime (forward + backward) as a function of context length, with bar heights normalized to FlashAttention-2 Triton (lower is better) and decomposed into forward and backward contributions.

As expected, AdaSplash is slower than FlashAttention-2 in the forward pass due to the additional passes required to compute the normalization threshold τ\tau (phases 1, 2, and 3 in §3.3). However, as context length increases, block sparsity naturally emerges, reducing the forward pass gap. In the backward pass, even at shorter contexts, existing sparsity already yields faster runtimes for AdaSplash-2, with the advantage increasing at longer contexts. Since the backward pass dominates training time, these gains are substantial. This suggests that as models scale to longer contexts, AdaSplash-2 can translate naturally emerging sparsity into training efficiency gains, contrasting with the dense nature of softmax-based attention.

4.3 Language Modeling Benchmarks

To evaluate the effectiveness of α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } attention in language modeling tasks, we train 350M and 1B parameters versions of the LLaMA-3 architecture (Grattafiori et al., 2024) using AdaSplash-2 with α=1.5\alpha=1.5. Our experimental design focuses on general capabilities and long-context performance and, thus, has two distinct settings: (i) one version that does pretraining from scratch for 50B tokens from the DCLM-Edu dataset (Allal et al., 2025), and (ii) an alternative version with a context extension phase with the ProLong (Gao et al., 2025) methodology in the final 20% of tokens, endowing our models with 32K context length. Furthermore, following Vasylenko et al. (2025), who show that RoPE can be suboptimal for entmax attention, we also evaluate their proposed positional encoding scheme, NAPE: within each layer, half of the heads use no positional encoding (NoPE; Kazemnejad et al. 2023) and the other half use ALiBi (Press et al., 2022). We compare AdaSplash-2 runs against softmax baselines with RoPE (Su et al., 2024) and with NAPE to ensure a fair comparison. Additional experimental details are provided in §D.

Long-context results.

We start by investigating the performance of our models on the full RULER benchmark (Hsieh et al., 2024), evaluated up to 32K context length. The results are presented in Table 1. Overall, α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } with NAPE achieves the strongest average performance across all sequence lengths, outperforming both softmax baselines. Among the different tasks, we note that the gains are particularly pronounced on Variable Tracking (VT)—a core subproblem underlying complex reasoning (Feng and Steinhardt, 2024; Dai et al., 2024)—as well as on common and frequent word extraction (CWE and FWE), which require precise aggregation of the relevant input spans.

Next, we evaluate the models’ in-context learning (ICL) performance using the ICL subset from the HELMET benchmark (Yen et al., 2025), which measures few-shot performance across increasing context lengths. Table 2 shows that α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } substantially improves ICL accuracy, especially when paired with NAPE, achieving the highest average score at every tested context length and outperforming softmax baselines. Notably, while all models improve as the context grows from 8K to 32K, we observe particularly large gains with α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } + NAPE, suggesting that sparsity helps the model in leveraging the relevant in-context examples, reinforcing the finding that α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } + NAPE constitutes a strong synergy for long-context modeling.

Short-context results.

For evaluating short-context performance, we follow the few-shot prompting strategy under the OLMES evaluation standard (Gu et al., 2025). The results are shown in Table 3. We first observe a substantial perplexity gap between softmax and α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } models on LAMBADA (LMB). Second, we note that α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } models are on par or better across the board on accuracy-based downstream tasks at both model scales (350M and 1B params.). Taken together, these results highlight the strengths of sparse attention by not just outperforming dense models on long-context settings, but also on short-context tasks.

5 Related Works

α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } computation.

Exact computation exists for special cases such as α∈{1.5,2}\alpha\in\{1.5,2\} using sorting-based solvers (Duchi et al., 2008; Condat, 2016; Peters et al., 2019). For general α\alpha, the normalization τ\tau can be computed using root-finding procedures (Blondel et al., 2019). However, these approaches remain suboptimal due to slow convergence or reliance on complex data structures and sorting operations, which are difficult to optimize for hardware.

Sparse attention mechanisms.

Sparse attention has been widely studied through fixed sparsity patterns (Zaheer et al., 2020; Beltagy et al., 2020). Recent methods aim for data-dependent sparsity, commonly via top-kk selection followed by softmax over the selected subset (Yuan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Nawrot et al., 2025). Top-kk is attractive for inference but can be unstable in training due to discontinuities. In contrast, α\alpha-entmax induces exact, differentiable, input-adaptive sparse attention. AdaSplash-2 focuses on making α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } attention efficient during training; while extending it to inference is non-trivial as the forward pass requires multiple key scans, and we leave a fully optimized inference kernel for future work.

GPU-aware attention for training.

FlashAttention and its successors (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2024; Shah et al., 2024) provide highly optimized CUDA kernels for softmax attention via fused normalization and tiled accumulation that exploit GPU memory hierarchies. FlexAttention (Dong et al., 2024) offers a programmable interface for custom masks/score modifications while using similar fused, tiled execution. AdaSplash (Gonçalves et al., 2025) offers a hardware-aware implementation of α\alpha-entmax attention by solving τ\tau with iterative refinement, but incurs considerable overhead due to repeated scans over keys and naive block-masking.

Long-context modeling.

A growing body of work studies why transformer performance degrades as context length grows, attributing failures to the softmax function itself such as attention dispersion (Zhai et al., 2023; Veličković et al., 2025) and representational collapse (Barbero et al., 2024; Arroyo et al., 2025). Complementary lines improve extrapolation through positional bias design (Press et al., 2022; Jelassi et al., 2024) and through length/entropy-aware scaling (Peng et al., 2024; Nakanishi, 2025; Zhang et al., 2024). In this context, a sparse learnable-temperature alternative with α\alpha-entmax have been proposed as a direct way to mitigate these issues (Vasylenko et al., 2025).

6 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced AdaSplash-2, a hardware-aware efficient implementation of α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } attention. Our key idea is to construct a compact histogram of streamed attention scores in on-chip SRAM, producing a strong initialization for the α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } threshold τ\tau, and reducing refinement to a small (typically 1-2) number of steps while integrating naturally with GPU execution. To leverage sparsity, AdaSplash-2 uses a lightweight bitpacked block mask to skip zero blocks efficiently. Empirically, AdaSplash-2 delivers training speedups over prior α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } kernels and, in moderate-to-high block-sparsity regimes, matches or exceeds FlashAttention-2, with gains driven primarily by a substantially faster backward pass. In language modeling, α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } models match or improve short-context performance and deliver clear gains on long-context evaluations.

Impact Statement

Our method, AdaSplash-2, provides an efficient implementation of α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } attention. Efficient attention mechanisms are crucial for scaling transformers to handle long-context sequences. As a result, the improved efficiency has potential applications in large-scale NLP applications, especially in cases where sparsity can be leveraged to reduce computational costs such as in long-context modeling. We do not foresee direct societal consequences from our method itself, but its integration into decision-making models may still reflect biases in training data. As such, we encourage careful evaluation when deploying models trained with AdaSplash-2 in high-stakes applications, ensuring that efficiency gains do not overcome ethical concerns.

Appendix A α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } Transformation

The α\alpha-entmax transformation of a score vector 𝒛∈ℝn\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is defined as follows (Peters et al., 2019):

α-entmax(𝒛):=argmax𝒑∈△n𝒑⊤𝒛+Hα(𝒑),△n:={𝒑∈ℝn:𝒑≥𝟎,𝟏⊤𝒑=1},\alpha\text{-entmax}(\bm{z}):=\arg\max_{\bm{p}\in\triangle_{n}}\bm{p}^{\top}\bm{z}+H_{\alpha}(\bm{p}),\quad\triangle_{n}:=\{\bm{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\,:\,\bm{p}\geq\mathbf{0},\mathbf{1}^{\top}\bm{p}=1\}, (12)

where Hα​(𝒑)H_{\alpha}(\bm{p}) is the Tsallis(α\alpha) entropy (Tsallis, 1988). Solving the optimization problem above corresponds to finding a threshold τ\tau so that 𝒑⋆\bm{p}^{\star} sums to 11. Given τ\tau, we can easily evaluate α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } as per Equation 3, which we re-state here for easiness:

α​-entmax ​(𝒛)=[(α−1)​𝒛−τ​𝟏]+1/α−1,\alpha\text{-entmax }(\bm{z})=[(\alpha-1)\bm{z}-\tau\bm{1}]_{+}^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{\alpha-1}}}, (13)

where [⋅]+[\cdot]_{+} is the ReLU function. Figure 5 illustrates how α​-entmax ​(𝒛)\alpha\text{-entmax }(\bm{z}) behaves for different choices of α\alpha. From the equation above, it is clear that coordinates with (α−1)​si≤τ(\alpha-1)s_{i}\leq\tau become exactly zero. In other words, α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } yields dynamic sparsity, where the pattern of zeros depends on the input. However, this flexibility comes at a computational cost: unlike softmax, α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } does not have a direct closed-form solution but rather requires more involved methods, which we discuss next.

α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } computation.

Order-based algorithms have only been proposed for α=2\alpha=2 (Michelot, 1986; Duchi et al., 2008; Condat, 2016) and α=1.5\alpha=1.5 (Peters et al., 2019). This family of algorithms builds upon the equivalence between τ\tau and the “active set”, denoted as 𝒮={j:zj>τ}\mathcal{S}=\{j:z_{j}>\tau\}. At τ⋆\tau^{\star}, this set indexes the nonzero terms in the expression of ff, or, equivalently, the nonzero elements in the α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } output. If the active set contains an index, it must contain all indices with greater or equal value, so there are nn possible active sets 𝒮1,…,𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{S}_{n}, where contains the indices of the kk largest values of 𝒛\bm{z}. Moreover, since the output must be a valid probability distribution, 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k} is never empty. At the true support size k⋆k^{\star}, we have

f⁡(τ)=fk⋆​(τ)≔−1+∑j∈𝒮k⋆(zj−τ)1/α−1.f(\tau)=f_{k^{\star}}(\tau)\coloneqq-1+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}_{k^{\star}}}(z_{j}-\tau)^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{\alpha-1}}}. (14)

Note that the ReLU function is no longer necessary as all terms are strictly positive. Finding the root of fkf_{k} for any kk can be done efficiently in the case of α=2\alpha=2 (linear equation) and α=1.5\alpha=1.5 (quadratic equation).

In contrast, root-finding algorithms apply for all values of α\alpha. Since max⁡(𝒛)=1\max(\bm{z})=1, following Peters et al. (2019), we have

0≤τ⋆≤1−n1−α.0\leq\tau^{\star}\leq 1-n^{1-\alpha}. (15)

Moreover, since ff is continuous and f⁡(0)≤0f(0)\leq 0 and f⁡(1−n1−α)≥0f(1-n^{1-\alpha})\geq 0, the root must be found in the interval. Blondel et al. (2019) propose a bisection or binary search approach to finding τ⋆\tau^{\star}. Similar in spirit, Gonçalves et al. (2025) introduces a GPU-oriented solver of α\alpha-entmax that uses a hybrid Halley-bisection method, which combines the fast local convergence of higher-order root-finding (Scavo and Thoo, 1995) with the convergence guarantees of bisection.

Appendix B Proofs

Throughout, we let α>1\alpha>1, represent scores as 𝒔∈ℝn\bm{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and we work with centered and scaled scores 𝒛=(α−1)​𝒔−(m−1)​𝟏\bm{z}=(\alpha-1)\bm{s}-(m-1)\bm{1}, where m=(α−1)​max⁡(𝒔)m=(\alpha-1)\max(\bm{s}), which ensures max⁡(𝒛)=1\max(\bm{z})=1. Also, we recall from Equation 15 that τ≥max⁡(𝒛)−1=0\tau\geq\max(\bm{z})-1=0 and τ≤max⁡(𝒛)−n1−α=1−n1−α\tau\leq\max(\bm{z})-n^{1-\alpha}=1-n^{1-\alpha}.

B.1 Proof of Proposition 3.2

Proof of Proposition 3.2.

We divide the proof in four parts.

Step 1: Establishing the sandwich inequality.

By construction of the binning scheme, for any score zj∈[0,1]z_{j}\in[0,1] assigned to bin kk, we have:

kB≤zj<k+1B,\frac{k}{B}\leq z_{j}<\frac{k+1}{B}, (16)

which implies:

bj≤zj<bj+h,where ​h=1B,b_{j}\leq z_{j}<b_{j}+h,\quad\text{where }h=\frac{1}{B}, (17)

where bj≔kBb_{j}\coloneqq\frac{k}{B} denotes the left edge of the bin to which zjz_{j} is assigned.

For scores zj<0z_{j}<0, we have [zj−τ]+=0=[bj−τ]+[z_{j}-\tau]_{+}=0=[b_{j}-\tau]_{+} for all τ>0\tau>0, so these scores do not affect the proof. Consider the function ϕ⁡(t)=[t]+1α−1\phi(t)=[t]_{+}^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}} for t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, which is monotone non-decreasing and continuous for α>1\alpha>1. For any fixed τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1], using the monotonicity of ϕ\phi and inequality in Eq. 17:

bj−τ\displaystyle b_{j}-\tau ≤zj−τ<bj+h−τ\displaystyle\leq z_{j}-\tau<b_{j}+h-\tau (18)
⟹[bj−τ]+\displaystyle\implies\quad[b_{j}-\tau]_{+} ≤[zj−τ]+<[bj+h−τ]+\displaystyle\leq[z_{j}-\tau]_{+}<[b_{j}+h-\tau]_{+} (19)
⟹ϕ⁡(bj−τ)\displaystyle\implies\quad\phi(b_{j}-\tau) ≤ϕ⁡(zj−τ)<ϕ⁡(bj+h−τ).\displaystyle\leq\phi(z_{j}-\tau)<\phi(b_{j}+h-\tau). (20)

The strict inequality on the right holds because: if zj−τ>0z_{j}-\tau>0, then zj<bj+hz_{j}<b_{j}+h implies zj−τ<bj+h−τz_{j}-\tau<b_{j}+h-\tau, and ϕ\phi is strictly increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty).

Summing over all j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n:

∑j=1nϕ⁡(bj−τ)≤∑j=1nϕ⁡(zj−τ)<∑j=1nϕ⁡(bj+h−τ).\sum_{j=1}^{n}\phi(b_{j}-\tau)\leq\sum_{j=1}^{n}\phi(z_{j}-\tau)<\sum_{j=1}^{n}\phi(b_{j}+h-\tau). (21)

Subtracting 1 from each term:

fh​(τ)≤f⁡(τ)<fh​(τ−h),∀τ∈[0,1],f_{h}(\tau)\leq f(\tau)<f_{h}(\tau-h),\quad\forall\tau\in[0,1], (22)

where we used the fact that:

∑j=1nϕ⁡(bj+h−τ)=∑j=1nϕ⁡(bj−(τ−h))=fh​(τ−h)+1.\sum_{j=1}^{n}\phi(b_{j}+h-\tau)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\phi(b_{j}-(\tau-h))=f_{h}(\tau-h)+1. (23)

Step 2: Properties of ff and fhf_{h}.

Both f⁡(τ)f(\tau) and fh​(τ)f_{h}(\tau) are:

  • •

    Continuous on [0,1][0,1]

  • •

    Strictly decreasing on [0,1][0,1] (since ϕ\phi is strictly increasing where positive)

  • •

    Satisfy f⁡(0)>0f(0)>0 and f⁡(1)<0f(1)<0 (similarly for fhf_{h})

By the intermediate value theorem, there exist unique roots:

τ⋆\displaystyle\tau^{\star} :f(τ⋆)=0,\displaystyle:\quad f(\tau^{\star})=0, (24)
τh\displaystyle\tau_{h} :fh(τh)=0.\displaystyle:\quad f_{h}(\tau_{h})=0. (25)

Step 3: Bounding τh\tau_{h} relative to τ⋆\tau^{\star}.

Evaluating the sandwich inequality in Eq. 22 at τ=τ⋆\tau=\tau^{\star}:

fh​(τ⋆)≤f⁡(τ⋆)<fh​(τ⋆−h).f_{h}(\tau^{\star})\leq f(\tau^{\star})<f_{h}(\tau^{\star}-h). (26)

Since f⁡(τ⋆)=0f(\tau^{\star})=0, we have:

fh​(τ⋆)≤0<fh​(τ⋆−h).f_{h}(\tau^{\star})\leq 0<f_{h}(\tau^{\star}-h). (27)

Because fhf_{h} is strictly decreasing and continuous, and fh​(τ⋆−h)>0f_{h}(\tau^{\star}-h)>0 while fh​(τ⋆)≤0f_{h}(\tau^{\star})\leq 0, there must exist a unique τh∈[τ⋆−h,τ⋆]\tau_{h}\in[\tau^{\star}-h,\tau^{\star}] such that fh​(τh)=0f_{h}(\tau_{h})=0.

More precisely:

  • •

    If fh​(τ⋆)<0f_{h}(\tau^{\star})<0, then τh∈(τ⋆−h,τ⋆)\tau_{h}\in(\tau^{\star}-h,\tau^{\star}) by the intermediate value theorem.

  • •

    If fh​(τ⋆)=0f_{h}(\tau^{\star})=0, then τh=τ⋆\tau_{h}=\tau^{\star}.

In both cases, we have:

τ⋆−h<τh≤τ⋆.\tau^{\star}-h<\tau_{h}\leq\tau^{\star}. (28)

Step 4: Error bound.

The absolute error is:

|τ⋆−τh|=τ⋆−τh≤h=1B.|\tau^{\star}-\tau_{h}|=\tau^{\star}-\tau_{h}\leq h=\frac{1}{B}. (29)

This completes the proof. ∎

The proof shows that the histogram approximation is conservative as it never overestimates τ⋆\tau^{\star}, which means τh≤τ⋆\tau_{h}\leq\tau^{\star}. This ensures that the approximate solution produces a sparsity pattern that preserves the support of the real solution—an useful property for safe block-masking.

B.2 Proof of Proposition 3.2

We divided the proof of Proposition 3.2 into two parts: (i) continuous differentiability of the threshold map ff, and (ii) continuous differentiability of the α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } transformation (from scores into probabilities). Throughout, we assume α>1\alpha>1, and work with translated and scaled scores 𝒛=(α−1)​𝒔−(m−1)​𝟏\bm{z}=(\alpha-1)\bm{s}-(m-1)\bm{1} where m=(α−1)​max⁡(𝒔)m=(\alpha-1)\max(\bm{s}). The domain of possible such scores after translation is D={𝒛∈ℝn:max⁡(𝒛)=1}D=\{\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\max(\bm{z})=1\}. Scaling and centering are continuous smooth operations and thus composing with them does not affect the continuity of any order of differentiation. We denote the active set induced by a threshold τ\tau as 𝒮τ≔{i∈[n]:zi>τ}\mathcal{S}_{\tau}\coloneqq\{i\in[n]:z_{i}>\tau\}.

Part (i): continuity of ff.

Given the active set 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}_{\tau}, the derivatives of ff have the form:

f⁡(τ)\displaystyle f(\tau) =−1+∑i∈𝒮τ(zi−τ)1α−1\displaystyle=-1+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{\tau}}\left(z_{i}-\tau\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}} (30)
f′​(τ)\displaystyle f^{\prime}(\tau) =−1α−1∑i∈𝒮τ(zi−τ)1α−1−1\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{\tau}}\left(z_{i}-\tau\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}-1} (31)
f′′​(τ)\displaystyle f^{\prime\prime}(\tau) =1α−1​(1α−1−1)​∑i∈𝒮τ(zi−τ)1α−1−2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\left(\frac{1}{\alpha-1}-1\right)\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{\tau}}\left(z_{i}-\tau\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}-2} (32)
f(k)​(τ)\displaystyle f^{(k)}(\tau) =(−1)k​[∏i=0k−1(1α−1−i)]​∑i∈𝒮τ(zi−τ)1α−1−k\displaystyle=(-1)^{k}\left[\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\left(\frac{1}{\alpha-1}-i\right)\right]\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{\tau}}\left(z_{i}-\tau\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}-k} (33)

We can study the continuity of any such derivative by considering the sum

sk​(τ)≔∑i∈𝒮τ(zi−τ)1α−1−k,s_{k}(\tau)\coloneqq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{\tau}}\left(z_{i}-\tau\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}-k}, (34)

because every term can be written as a continuous transformation of sks_{k}. For a small enough ϵ>0\epsilon>0, Sτ+ϵ=𝒮τS_{\tau+\epsilon}=\mathcal{S}_{\tau}. As a sum of continuous functions we therefore have

limϵ→0+sk​(τ+ϵ)=sk​(τ).\lim_{\epsilon\to 0_{+}}s_{k}(\tau+\epsilon)=s_{k}(\tau). (35)

If τ≠zi\tau\neq z_{i} for any i∈[n]i\in[n] then Sτ−ϵ=𝒮τS_{\tau-\epsilon}=\mathcal{S}_{\tau} also, so the only possible discontinuities are when τ=zi\tau=z_{i} for some ii. In this case, ziz_{i} enters the support (and thus the sum) alongside any other tied zj=ziz_{j}=z_{i}. Let’s say the value ziz_{i} appears ni≥1n_{i}\geq 1 times in the vector. We can write

sk​(τ−ϵ)\displaystyle s_{k}(\tau-\epsilon) =∑j∈Sτ−ϵ(zj−τ+ϵ)1α−1−k\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in S_{\tau-\epsilon}}\left(z_{j}-\tau+\epsilon\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}-k} (36)
=∑j∈𝒮τ(zj−τ+ϵ)1α−1−k+ni​(zi−τ+ϵ)1α−1−k\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}_{\tau}}\left(z_{j}-\tau+\epsilon\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}-k}+n_{i}\left(z_{i}-\tau+\epsilon\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}-k} (37)

Taking the limit to 0, the sum is a sum of continuous functions and so we have

limϵ→0+sk​(τ−ϵ)\displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\to 0_{+}}s_{k}(\tau-\epsilon) =sk​(τ)+limϵ→0+ni​(zi−τ+ϵ)1α−1−k\displaystyle=s_{k}(\tau)+\lim_{\epsilon\to 0_{+}}n_{i}(z_{i}-\tau+\epsilon)^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}-k} (38)
=sk​(τ)+ni​limϵ→0+ϵ1α−1−k\displaystyle=s_{k}(\tau)+n_{i}\lim_{\epsilon\to 0_{+}}\epsilon^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}-k} (39)

It follows that sks_{k} is continuous at τ\tau iff. (α−1)−1−k>0(\alpha-1)^{-1}-k>0. In particular:

  • •

    f⁡(τCLOSEf(\tau) is continuous when 1<α1<\alpha.

  • •

    f′​(τCLOSEf^{\prime}(\tau) is continuous when 1<α<21<\alpha<2.

  • •

    f′′​(τCLOSEf^{\prime\prime}(\tau) is continuous when 1<α<3/21<\alpha<3/2, and so on.

Part (ii): continuity of α\alpha-entmax.

Let

Fα​(𝒛,τ)=−1+∑i∈𝒮τ(zi−τ)1α−1.F_{\alpha}(\bm{z},\tau)=-1+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{\tau}}(z_{i}-\tau)^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}}. (40)

Recall that, by continuity and monotonicity of ff, for any 𝒛\bm{z} there is a unique τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1] such that Fα​(𝒛,τ)=0F_{\alpha}(\bm{z},\tau)=0; denote by g⁡(𝒛)g(\bm{z}) the function mapping 𝒛\bm{z} to that corresponding unique root τ\tau.66 6 At the root the active set is nonempty: if 𝒮τ=∅\mathcal{S}_{\tau}=\varnothing, then Fα​(𝒛,τ)=−1≠0F_{\alpha}(\bm{z},\tau)=-1\neq 0. Equivalently, since max⁡(𝒛)=1\max(\bm{z})=1, any root satisfies τ<1\tau<1 (because Fα​(𝒛,τ)=−1F_{\alpha}(\bm{z},\tau)=-1 for τ≥1\tau\geq 1). If α∈(1,2)\alpha\in(1,2), from the continuity of ff shown above, we have that FαF_{\alpha} is 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1}. The condition that the jacobian be nonsingular in this case is equivalent to f′​(τ)≠0f^{\prime}(\tau)\neq 0 (Eq. 31). The terms in the sum sks_{k} are all positive. For τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1] the sum contains at least one term corresponding to the maximum (scaled) score and thus f′​(τ)<0f^{\prime}(\tau)<0, confirming nonsingularity. The conditions of the implicit function theorem (Dontchev and Rockafellar, 2014, Thm. 1B.1) are therefore satisfied, which implies the solution mapping gg is 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} for any 𝒛∈D\bm{z}\in D. Since α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } can be written coordinate-wise as

pj​(𝒛)=[zj−g⁡(𝒛)]+1α−1,p_{j}(\bm{z})=\left[z_{j}-g(\bm{z})\right]_{+}^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}}, (41)

its (almost everywhere) gradient with respect to 𝒛\bm{z} is

∇pj​(𝒛)=1α−1​[zj−g⁡(𝒛)]+1α−1−1​(𝒆j−∇g​(𝒛)),\nabla p_{j}(\bm{z})=\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\left[z_{j}-g(\bm{z})\right]_{+}^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}-1}\left(\bm{e}_{j}-\nabla g(\bm{z})\right), (42)

and ∇pj​(𝒛)=𝟎\nabla p_{j}(\bm{z})=\bm{0} whenever zj<g⁡(𝒛)z_{j}<g(\bm{z}). For 1<α<21<\alpha<2 this function is a composition/product of continuous functions, and thus it is continuous (Rudin, 1976, Theorems 4.7 & 4.9). Therefore, for this range of α\alpha, the “almost everywhere” above becomes “everywhere”.

Furthermore, by the higher-order extension of the implicit function theorem (Dontchev and Rockafellar, 2014, Prop. 1B.5), we can repeat this argument for higher-order derivatives. When α<k+1k\alpha<\frac{k+1}{k}, from the result in the first part we have Fα∈𝒞kF_{\alpha}\in\mathcal{C}^{k} This implies gg is also 𝒞k\mathcal{C}^{k}.

Applying the same argument coordinate-wise, it follows that α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } is 𝒞k\mathcal{C}^{k} whenever 1<α<k+1k1<\alpha<\frac{k+1}{k}. Indeed, as α→1+\alpha\to 1_{+} we recover softmax, which is 𝒞∞\mathcal{C}^{\infty}.

Appendix C AdaSplash-2 Implementation Details

This appendix provides a detailed exposition of AdaSplash-2’s implementation, including the bitpacking schemes that enable efficient histogram construction and block mask traversal. We begin by establishing notation (§C.1), then describe the histogram construction and capacity analysis (§C.2), block mask encoding (§C.4), and overflow handling strategies (§C.5).

C.1 Notation and Problem Setup

Sequence and Tiling Parameters.

We work with input sequences of length nn, head dimension dd, batch size BB, and NHN_{H} attention heads. The sequences are partitioned into tiles: query tiles of size BrB_{r} and key/value tiles of size BcB_{c}, yielding Tr=⌈n/Br⌉T_{r}=\lceil n/B_{r}\rceil query tiles and Tc=⌈n/Bc⌉T_{c}=\lceil n/B_{c}\rceil key/value tiles. Throughout, we use indices i∈[Tr]i\in[T_{r}] for query tiles and j∈[Tc]j\in[T_{c}] for key tiles.

Histogram Parameters.

The histogram has shape ℋ∈ℕBr×B\mathcal{H}\in\mathbb{N}^{B_{r}\times B}. To avoid atomics or reductions, we first accumulate the counts in local histograms ℋlocal\mathcal{H}^{\text{local}} private to each position, providing Br×BcB_{r}\times B_{c} parallel accumulators. Our local histograms use BB bins encoded in a ww-bit unsigned integer (e.g., w=64w=64 for uint64), allocating b=w/Bb=w/B bits per bin. The bin width (resolution) is h=1/Bh=1/B.

Bitwise Operations.

We use standard notation for bit manipulation:

  • •

    x≪kx\ll k: Left shift by kk bits (multiply by 2k2^{k})

  • •

    x≫kx\gg k: Right shift by kk bits (divide by 2k2^{k}, rounded down)

  • •

    x∧yx\land y: Bitwise AND

  • •

    x∨yx\lor y: Bitwise OR

  • •

    popc​(x)\texttt{popc}(x): Population count (number of 1-bits)

  • •

    fns​(x,k)\texttt{fns}(x,k): Find first set bit at position ≥k\geq k

C.2 Histogram Construction and Bitpacking

The histogram construction in Algorithm 1 (Phase 2) is the computational core of AdaSplash-2’s threshold approximation. We now describe its implementation in detail.

Bitpacked Encoding Scheme.

Each local histogram accumulator ℋi​klocal∈{0,1,…,2w−1}\mathcal{H}^{\text{local}}_{ik}\in\{0,1,\ldots,2^{w}-1\} encodes BB bin counts by partitioning its ww bits into BB equal segments of b=w/Bb=w/B bits each. The value ℋi​jlocal\mathcal{H}^{\text{local}}_{ij} can be decomposed as:

ℋi​jlocal=∑t=0B−1ck​ 2k​b,where ​ck∈[0,2b−1]​ is the local counts for bin ​t.\mathcal{H}^{\text{local}}_{ij}\;=\;\sum_{t=0}^{B-1}c_{k}\,2^{kb},\quad\text{where }c_{k}\in[0,2^{b}-1]\text{ is the local counts for bin }t. (43)

Figure 6 illustrates this structure for B=8B=8 bins with b=8b=8 bits per bin in a uint64.

Accumulation.

For each entry Zi​jZ_{ij} (see Eq. 6), we compute the corresponding bin,

ki​j=min⁡(max⁡(⌊B​Zi​j⌋,0),B−1).k_{ij}\;=\;\min\!\big(\max(\lfloor B\,Z_{ij}\rfloor,0),\,B-1\big). (44)

Each update increments the respective bit field inside the packed integer:

ℋi​jlocal←ℋi​jlocal+ 1[Zi​j≥0]⋅(1≪(bki,j)).\mathcal{H}^{\text{local}}_{ij}\;\leftarrow\;\mathcal{H}^{\text{local}}_{ij}\;+\;\mathbf{1}[Z_{ij}\geq 0]\cdot\big(1\ll(b\,k_{i,j})\big). (45)

In Triton, this update can be achieved with a shift plus an integer addition.

Extraction and Aggregation.

After accumulation, we extract the count for bin k∈{0,…,B−1}k\in\{0,\dots,B-1\} from the packed uint64 word by shifting and masking. Let ℬb=2b−1\mathcal{B}_{b}=2^{b}-1 be the bb-bit mask (i.e., bb consecutive 1-bits). Then, we can aggregate across the BcB_{c} parallel accumulators (over jj) to obtain per-query bin counts

ℋi​k=∑j(ℋi​jlocal≫(k​b))∧ℬb.\mathcal{H}_{ik}\;=\;\sum_{j}\big(\mathcal{H}^{\text{local}}_{ij}\gg(k\,b)\big)\;\land\;\mathcal{B}_{b}. (46)

In Triton, we vectorize the shift-and-mask over bb using a compile-time range.

C.3 Histogram initialization

With the final histogram ℋ\mathcal{H} obtained, we can solve the approximate problem (see Eq. 9) using a modified version of the sorting-based algorithms discussed in Section 2.4. The τ0\tau_{0} and bracket [τlo,τhi][\tau_{\text{lo}},\tau_{\text{hi}}] obtained from this phase will be used for posterior refinement. Here, we present the algorithms in detail.

Case α∈{1.5,2.0}\alpha\in\{1.5,2.0\}.

As the counts are conveniently sorted in the histogram ℋ\mathcal{H}, we scan bins in descending order, k∈[B−1,..,0]k\in[B-1,..,0]. We maintain prefix sums over the active (ordered) set 𝒫=[B−1,B−2,…,k]\mathcal{P}=[B-1,B-2,\ldots,k]:

S0=∑k∈𝒫ℋk,S1=∑k∈𝒫ℋk⋅kB,S2=∑k∈𝒫ℋk⋅(kB)2.\displaystyle S_{0}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{P}}\mathcal{H}_{k},\quad S_{1}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{P}}\mathcal{H}_{k}\cdot\frac{k}{B},\quad S_{2}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{P}}\mathcal{H}_{k}\cdot\left(\frac{k}{B}\right)^{2}. (47)

Intuitively, we start with an empty set where fh​(τ)=−1f_{h}(\tau)=-1. Iteratively, we add contributions from the next bin (k=B−1k=B-1, then k=B−2k=B-2, …) while evaluating f⁡(τ=k/B)f(\tau=k/B). If adding the contribution of a bin, kk, cause f⁡(τ)f(\tau) to be positive, it means that the root is between the values k/B<τ<(k+1)/Bk/B<\tau<(k+1)/B. When that set 𝒫k⋆\mathcal{P}_{k}^{\star} is found, we can drop the ReLU, [⋅]+[\cdot]_{+}, and solve for τ\tau. Example for α=2.0\alpha=2.0:

∑k∈𝒫k⋆ℋk​(kB−τ)=1\displaystyle\sum_{k\in\mathcal{P}_{k}^{\star}}\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(\frac{k}{B}-\tau\right)=1
∑k∈𝒫k⋆ℋk​kB⏟S1−τ​∑k∈𝒫k⋆ℋk⏟S0=1⟹τ=S1−1S0\displaystyle\underbrace{\sum_{k\in\mathcal{P}_{k}^{\star}}\mathcal{H}_{k}\frac{k}{B}}_{S_{1}}-\,\tau\underbrace{\sum_{k\in\mathcal{P}_{k}^{\star}}\mathcal{H}_{k}}_{S_{0}}=1\implies\tau=\frac{S_{1}-1}{S_{0}}

General α\alpha.

For a general α\alpha, we can find τ⋆\tau^{\star} by using any method originally developed for α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax }. However, instead of iterating over the actual scores, we can cheaply iterate over the histogram ℋ\mathcal{H}.

C.4 Block Mask Encoding and Traversal

After computing the threshold τ\tau in Phase 3 of Algorithm 1, we construct a binary mask ℳ∈{0,1}Tr×Tc\mathcal{M}\in\{0,1\}^{T_{r}\times T_{c}} indicating which tile pairs (i,j)(i,j) contain non-zero attention weights. Naively storing this as a boolean tensor would require Tr×TcT_{r}\times T_{c} bytes. Instead, we use bitpacking encoded in int32 to reduce memory by a factor of 32×32\times. That is, we pack 32 consecutive column indices into a single int32, yielding a compact representation ℳpacked∈ℤTr×⌈Tc/32⌉\mathcal{M}^{\text{packed}}\in\mathbb{Z}^{T_{r}\times\lceil T_{c}/32\rceil} defined by:

ℳi,⌊j/32⌋packed=∑k=031ℳi,32​⌊j/32⌋+k⋅2k.\mathcal{M}^{\text{packed}}_{i,\lfloor j/32\rfloor}=\sum_{k=0}^{31}\mathcal{M}_{i,32\lfloor j/32\rfloor+k}\cdot 2^{k}. (48)

As a result, each bit in ℳi,mpacked\mathcal{M}^{\text{packed}}_{i,m} indicates whether the corresponding tile pair has non-zero weights.

Efficient Traversal with GPU Instructions.

To iterate through active tiles, we use two GPU-native instructions:

  1. 1.

    popc​(ℳi,mpacked)\texttt{popc}(\mathcal{M}^{\text{packed}}_{i,m}): Returns the number of set bits (active tiles) in the int32.

  2. 2.

    fns​(ℳi,mpacked,k)\texttt{fns}(\mathcal{M}^{\text{packed}}_{i,m},k): Find the n-th set bit given by offset kk.

The traversal procedure processes only the |ℳ||\mathcal{M}| non-zero tiles rather than all Tr×TcT_{r}\times T_{c} potential tiles. Concretely, for each packed word index mm, we iterate only over set bits (active key blocks) using popc to count and fns to locate bits. If bit_pos is the position of a set bit within word mm, the corresponding key-block index is

j= 32​m+bit_pos.j\;=\;32m+\texttt{bit\_pos}. (49)

The operations operations are implemented via Triton’s inline PTX assembly, making the traversal cost negligible compared to the memory and compute operations. This traversal mechanism is used in Phase 4 of Algorithm 1 to load only the non-zero key and value tiles, and similarly in the backward pass to skip zero blocks.

C.5 Histogram Capacity and Overflow Handling

The bitpacking scheme naturally imposes capacity limits for our histogram since each bin can count up to 2b−12^{b}-1 items before overflow. With BcB_{c} parallel accumulators per query tile, the maximum capacity is:

Cmax=Bc×(2w/B−1).C_{\text{max}}=B_{c}\times(2^{w/B}-1). (50)

Table 4 summarizes capacity and resolution trade-offs for various configurations. The table reveals a fundamental trade-off: increasing BB improves threshold resolution (tighter bound in Proposition 3.2) but reduces capacity per bin. For sequences up to 16K tokens per query, uint64 with B=8B=8 provides excellent resolution (h=0.125h=0.125) while avoiding overflow. For longer sequences, we turn to an overflow mitigation strategy, which we describe next.77 7 We note that uint128 is already available in CUDA: https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/implementing-high-precision-decimal-arithmetic-with-cuda-int128/

Periodic Flush.

After processing CmaxC_{\text{max}} keys, we extract all bin counts, accumulate them into shared memory array of size (Tr×B)(T_{r}\times B), and reset the SRAM histogram to zero. Since each query processes TcT_{c} key tiles and the histogram saturates after 2b−12^{b}-1 tiles, the number of flushes required for a sequence of length nn is:

Nflush=⌈nBc×(2b−1)⌉=⌈Tc2b−1⌉.N_{\text{flush}}=\left\lceil\frac{n}{B_{c}\times(2^{b}-1)}\right\rceil=\left\lceil\frac{T_{c}}{2^{b}-1}\right\rceil. (51)

C.6 Backward Pass Algorithms

In the backward pass, we exploit the block mask ℳ\mathcal{M} to skip zero gradients, achieving asymptotic speedups when sparsity is high. The key difference from standard attention backpropagation is the use of the block mask ℳ\mathcal{M} (and its transpose ℳ⊤\mathcal{M}^{\top}) to iterate only over non-zero blocks. For |ℳ|≪Tr⋅Tc|\mathcal{M}|\ll T_{r}\cdot T_{c} (high sparsity), this provides order-of-magnitude speedups in the backward pass, offsetting the higher forward pass cost of AdaSplash-2 relative to FlashAttention-2.

Appendix D Language Modeling

We train our language models with the torchtitan library (Liang et al., 2025) and in a single node with 4x H100 NVIDIA GPUs. The models are trained for 50B tokens of DCLM-Edu data with the WSD scheduler (2000 warmup steps, stable until 80% of training and decay for the latter 10B tokens). Weight decay is set to 0.1 and maximum learning rate is set to 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} and 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} for 350M and 1B parameter models, respectively. Final learning rate is set to 10% of the maximum. Context length is set to 4096 tokens with an effective batch size of 524k tokens, resulting in 100k total steps. We decide to go beyond the Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022) optimal token counts since we saw steady increased model performance even with the additional tokens. Finally, for inference we use a simplified variant of AdaSplash-2 that operates on fully materialized logits 𝒛∈ℝn\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Despite its simplicity, in practice we found this approach to be faster than parallelizing over the K/V sequence dimension for the sequence lengths considered in this work.

Context-length extension.

For the long-context extension phase we swap the data mixture at the decay phase (10B tokens) with the ProLong dataset (Gao et al., 2025), keeping total training data at 50B tokens. Here, we increase the sequence length to 32k and keep the effective batch size fixed. For RoPE-based models, we increase their θ\theta from the 50k default to 800k, consistent with the ProLong methodology.

Evaluation.

For long-context we adopt both the full RULER benchmark (Hsieh et al., 2024) and the In-Context Learning subset of HELMET (Yen et al., 2025) which is a capability not covered by RULER. For evaluation in short-context tasks, we also include Lambada (Paperno et al., 2016; Radford et al., 2019) for evaluating perplexity, and drop BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019) from the evaluation mix following Olmo3 (Olmo et al., 2025). For completeness, we provide the results of all of our models on short-context benchmarks in Table 5. The results on RULER for the long-context adapted models are presented in Table 1, while the HELMET-ICL results can be seen in Table 2.

Discussion.

Overall, we see that extended models show a small degradation on short-context benchmarks, which is typical of long-context extension (Gao et al., 2025). However, the scenario flips when we look at Table 1, where we observe that our long-context procedure was effective and 32K-context models are able to complete tasks at 32K context length to an effective degree. Analysis of In-Context Learning capabilities (Table  2) between dense and sparse models further confirm the strengths of AdaSplash-2 as it outperforms softmax models across all evaluated sequence lengths.

D.1 Dense to Sparse Attention Conversion

Having established the efficacy and efficiency of sparse attention, we make a preliminary study of how to convert a pretrained softmax model into a α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } one. We do so via continued pretraining: starting from a 1B-parameter checkpoint trained with softmax + NAPE at 4K context length, we replace softmax with α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } (implemented with AdaSplash-2) and continue training for 10B tokens on Nemotron-CC-V2 (Basant et al., 2025), keeping the final learning rate unchanged. We focus only on 1B NAPE model variants due to the seemingly sub-optimality of RoPE for α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } attention. Table 6 shows the full results. Directly replacing softmax with α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } in the attention modules without any additional training results in a performance degradation but not a total collapse (see “Entmax (converted)” entry). After only 2B tokens, at 52B tokens in total, the converted checkpoint already outperforms the baseline softmax scores on average. Finally, we continue training the baselines to measure the total performance lost due to the conversion, evaluating after successive increases of 1B tokens. We observe that the finals results are roughly on par with the results obtained by softmax and α​-entmax \alpha\text{-entmax } models trained from scratch on the full 60B tokens. Overall, this strategy offers insight into a efficient recipe for building entmax-based models from existing softmax + NAPE checkpoints, which is particularly appealing for midtraining or long-context extension phases. Applying this methodology to other positional encodings or architectures could, additionally, require other adaptation phases (Gelberg et al., 2026).

Appendix E Attention Sparsity and Efficiency

Sparse attention patterns.

In Figure 7, we analyze emerging attention block sparsity in the 1B Entmax (NAPE) model trained up to 32K context length. We compute the average 64×6464\times 64 attention block sparsity ratios across 64 sequences sampled from the ProLong dataset, evaluated at multiple context lengths (4K, 8K, 16K, 32K, 64K and 128K). Across all context lengths, the sparsity pattern is strongly head-dependent. The first half of the heads (0-11; ALiBi) are consistently sparse across layers. In contrast, the second half (12-23; NoPE) is comparatively dense at 4K, but develops structured sparsity as context grows, most notably in mid-to-late layers. The overall mean sparsity increases monotonically with context length, indicating that longer contexts are handled with less dense attention on average.

Context scaling experiment details.

We study the runtime behavior of AdaSplash-2 as context length increases using attention block sparsity patterns extracted from the 1B Entmax + NAPE model with 32k context length, reported in Table 1. To this end, we select a fixed transformer layer that exhibits high block sparsity and record its average block sparsity as a function of context length. For each context length, we benchmark AdaSplash-2 at the corresponding sparsity level, run forward and backward passes, and report average runtimes over repeated runs. Figure 4 reports the resulting average forward and backward runtimes as a function of context length.
